// Notes from the lab

Building ANT-4B and ANT-08B

Semantique · 24 Oct 2026 · 9 min read

What broke along the way.

ANT is a decision model. You give it a state, a question and a list of candidates, and it returns calibrated probabilities over those candidates plus a verdict: execute the top choice, or escalate to a human. It never generates text. The decoder behind it is used as an encoder, the trainable part is a small scoring head, and the output is meant for software that has to act.

We built two of them and open-sourced both:

  • ANT-4B on Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B — github.com/semantique-team/ant-4b
  • ANT-08B on Qwen/Qwen3.5-0.8B — github.com/semantique-team/ant-08b
  • the web playground that serves them — github.com/semantique-team/playground

This post is the development log: how the two models are trained, what the numbers look like, and the problems we hit between a working training script and something you can run on a laptop. The performance work on Apple Silicon, the MLX port and the quantization attempts get their own sections, because that is where most of the time went.

The model in one picture

Two encoders share one frozen Qwen3.5 decoder. The context encoder embeds state and question; the candidate encoder embeds each candidate. A scoring function turns the pair into one logit per candidate, a softmax with a fitted temperature turns logits into probabilities, and a risk/coverage policy fitted on validation data decides whether the top probability is good enough to act on.

Candidate count is variable (2 to 100+), so the same model routes a ticket to four departments or ranks sixty CVs. The scoring is permutation invariant, so reordering options does not move the probabilities. And candidates can be embedded once and cached, so a follow-up question over the same option set only pays for the context encoding.

Training: frozen backbone, 2.6M trainable parameters, one GPU

Both heads were trained on the same multitask dataset: 5,952 training rows, 688 validation, 648 test, 456 out-of-distribution, spread over 29 use cases in English and Italian (support routing, incident severity, expense category, bug component, email action, urgenza_ticket_it, approvazione_spese_it, and so on). Each row is a state, a question, its candidates and the labelled answer.

The backbone stays frozen. ANT-4B trains 2,632,704 parameters out of 4.2 billion; ANT-08B trains 1,053,696 out of 753 million. Three epochs, batch size 8, learning rate 2e-4, seed 7: the same recipe for both, so the comparison below is between backbones rather than between training runs. On a Kaggle T4 an epoch takes about 19 minutes for the 4B head and 9 minutes for the 0.8B one.

Train loss falls to about 0.005 for both models while validation loss keeps falling much more slowly. The head has enough capacity to memorize the training rows, so the validation curve is the honest one. The 0.8B model ends ahead on validation accuracy (0.757 against 0.731), which makes the next chart more interesting.

Held-out results: the 4B model earns its size on the hard cases

On the 648-row test split, ANT-4B reaches 0.739 accuracy with ECE 0.0555; ANT-08B reaches 0.674 with ECE 0.0609. On the out-of-distribution split both drop (0.597 and 0.570) and calibration degrades more for the small model (ECE 0.123 against 0.220). That OOD gap is the case the escalation policy exists for: when confidence falls below the fitted threshold, the model hands the decision back instead of guessing.

The per-use-case chart is where the aggregate gap comes from. The 0.8B model is competitive or better on several routing and classification tasks (order_intent, document_type, lead_quality, meeting_action, richiesta_assistenza_it). It falls apart on the tasks that need fine semantic discrimination: bug_component 0.70 against 0.33, project_status 0.50 against 0.28, candidate_screening 0.69 against 0.47, incident_severity 0.78 against 0.56.

At the bottom, transaction_risk is near chance for both models (0.125 and 0.000 on 8 test rows) and urgenza_ticket_it sits around 0.35 for both. More parameters will not fix those two. They are first on the list for the next data pass.

What broke getting the code to the GPU

Local training was a dead end. The Qwen3.5 architecture is a hybrid: 24 of its 32 layers are GatedDeltaNet linear attention, and the fused kernels for them (flash-linear-attention, causal-conv1d) are CUDA/Triton only. On a Mac they fall back to a reference PyTorch path that is correct and extremely slow. We stopped a local training run on an M3 with 16 GB and moved training to hosted GPUs; the laptop now only converts, serves and profiles. The two recipes we kept are train on Colab and train on Kaggle.

The working tree does not travel through git. Both guides assume the code you are shipping is the code you are testing, and a lot of it was uncommitted at the time. A clone or git archive silently drops exactly the files under test, so the workflow zips the working tree (minus .venv, models, runs) into a private Kaggle dataset or an upload to Colab. We then hit two small papercuts on the Kaggle side, both fixed in the docs: the notebook hardcoded one archive name, and it grabbed the first zip under /kaggle/input instead of the one we attached.

Interrupted runs left half-written checkpoints. A dropped Colab session can kill the process mid-write, and a partial ant_head.pt looks exactly like a finished one until you try to load it. Checkpoint and report writes are now atomic (write to a temporary file, then rename), the data loader rejects malformed rows up front (fewer than two candidates, or a label that is not among them), and the training logs avoid device-side scalar conversions that can deadlock a CUDA run. Training is still not resumable: the optimizer state is not saved, so the documented rule is to rerun into a new output directory rather than trust a partial head.

Comparisons between runs were silently wrong. The first local reference figures came from a 40-row gate sample (accuracy 0.725, ECE 0.1553) and the 2026-10-17 checkpoint was evaluated on a 392-row test split, while the current runs report on 648 rows. Any table mixing those numbers compares three different questions. Both training guides now state the split, row count and seed that a comparison must hold fixed, and this post only compares runs evaluated on the same 648-row split.

From 13 seconds to 370 milliseconds

The first working end-to-end prediction on the 4B model took about 13 seconds on the M3. Long enough that the playground was unusable, so we profiled before touching anything. Encoding dominated the profile, and the path was doing it twice. The fix was one fused single-pass encode (context and all candidates through the backbone in one forward), torch.inference_mode, and length bucketing at 64/128/256/512/1024 tokens so shapes are reused instead of recompiled. Loading plain fp16 without device_map also mattered: the device_map="mps" path crashed on this stack (a silent SIGTRAP in malloc), and the plain load is what ships.

Warm medians went from ~13,000 ms to 372 ms on a 14-token input and 373 ms on 53 tokens, about 8x. Longer inputs still cost: 1,446 ms at 210 tokens and 2,866 ms at 418. The first predict() call takes 1,681 ms because it compiles the bucket shapes.

The floor is the linear attention. With no fused kernels on MPS, the 24 GatedDeltaNet layers run the reference path and latency grows roughly linearly with length. Milliseconds on long inputs are not reachable for a 4.66B hybrid on a 16 GB machine today; the path there is the MLX backend, not more PyTorch tuning.

Quantization: two attempts, two different verdicts

We tried to shrink the model twice, on two different stacks, with opposite outcomes.

Metal 8-bit through transformers: off. It halves residency (3.80 GB with a bf16 load, 5.07 GB with fp16, against 8.42 GB for the plain load) and breaks the model. The accuracy gate on 40 test rows went from 0.725 to 0.325 with 27 of 40 argmax flips; per-row probability deltas came back NaN. Isolating the failure showed hidden states that are all zero under fp16 and NaN under bf16, while the same unquantized load is sane either way.

The evidence says this is not our loading code. On a tiny locally built Qwen3.5 text model the same quantizer and kernel are numerically correct (max deviation 5.08e-02, no zeros, no NaN), so the garbage is specific to the real 4B shapes. Two more findings from the same session: save_pretrained wrote a pre-quantized checkpoint without its quantization_config (we patched it by hand), reloading that checkpoint hung for ten minutes or segfaulted inside the MPS copy/cast kernel, and transformers pins version 1 of kernels-community/mlx-quantization-metal-kernels while version 2 exists. Loading and quantizing a 4B model on 16 GB of unified memory is also the moment the machine hard rebooted once.

So Metal 8-bit stays off, and we adopted a gate-first rule: no quantized number is real until scripts/compare_quantization.py passes against a fresh fp16 reference (tolerances 0.005 on accuracy, 0.02 on ECE, plus argmax-flip inspection).

MLX for the 0.8B model: working, with two bugs fixed. MLX is the serving backend that can actually reach the millisecond range on Apple Silicon, so we ported the ANT-08B backbone to it. Two bugs came out of the first port. The MLX TokenizerWrapper exposes encode() but is not callable like a Hugging Face tokenizer, so the batch path was encoding nothing; and hidden states had to be cast to mx.float32 before conversion to NumPy, otherwise the head scores garbage. Both are fixed and covered by tests.

Then we converted the 0.8B checkpoint at three precision levels and compared hidden states against the unquantized MLX reference.

8-bit is plausible: the folder shrinks from 1.4 GB to 782 MB and pooled cosine similarity of the hidden states stays at 0.9953. 4-bit is much lighter at 424 MB but the representations drift (cosine 0.7436), so it is marked experimental and disabled. These are hidden-state diagnostics, not decision-quality results: 8-bit replaces the default only after it passes the same accuracy gate as above, run against a Colab-trained ANT head.

What a decision looks like in the playground

The playground is a FastAPI server plus a Vite interface. You point it at one or more checkpoint directories, it lists their models, and each request runs through the same ANTPredictor the Python API uses. The screenshot shows a support ticket routed to the billing team at 43.9% against 36.0% for engineering support: the label matches the annotated answer, but the margin is narrow, so the policy says escalate rather than act.

What is still open

Both repositories are marked work in progress on purpose. Benchmarks and calibration guidance are not finished, transaction_risk and urgenza_ticket_it need better data, the Metal quantization failure deserves an upstream report with the tiny-model evidence, and the MLX 8-bit variant is waiting on its accuracy gate. The experiment log in each repo (ANT-4B, ANT-08B) lists what comes next: scorer comparisons against dot product, candidate-count scaling, cached candidate batches and multilingual calibration drift.
